Find the code for a task from a plain-language query (start here)

Usage:
  entire graph search --query "issue or concept" --repo . [--top-k 10] [--format text|json|ndjson|agent] [--head] [--profile fast|full] [--deep]

Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with source and file:line inline, budgeted to drop straight into context. This is the first move for almost every locate task.

By default search returns: ranked candidate fix sites (top hits as full function bodies), RELATED SITES, the COVERING TEST plus other tests over the same code (ALSO COVERING), SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL (every place the concept is named, tagged EDIT/CONSUMER/DOC), a VERIFY line (the narrowest test command for the file), and a CLOSED-SET WARNING when a switch over a sealed set would fail at runtime. The three reference blocks (container map, signature types, declaration card) are OFF by default because they cost turns in agent sessions; --reference-blocks all turns them on for interactive reading.

--top-k only changes how many results come back; --deep additionally runs the exhaustive sparse (BM25) pass and fuses it with the semantic ranking (slower, reads every eligible file).

Ranking returns one region per unit, which is right for code and wrong for whole prose documents: one markdown document can hold the answer across several distant regions. So for prose the unit is the SECTION, not the file — a document's headed sections are ranked against every other section on their own scores, exactly as independent files would be (--document-resolution ranks a document as one unit instead). Separately, and on prose of any shape including headed documents, when fewer distinct units match than --top-k asked for, the spare slots are spent returning finer regions of the same document as results of their own (multi-resolution retrieval) — strictly additive, so it never displaces a unit and never breaches --max-context-bytes. --single-resolution turns that off. The two stack: a headed document can be ranked by section AND have spare slots filled with promoted passages, so a prose payload may carry both.

Flags:
  --query <text>            The task or bug in one plain sentence (required)
  --repo <path>             Repository to search (default: current repo)
  --top-k <n>               Number of results to return (default: 10)
  --format text|json|ndjson|agent
                            Output format; text is tiered for reading, agent is compact (default: json)
  --head                    Search the committed tree (cached) instead of the working tree
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                            Parsing depth; use full for bug-fix/locate (call-graph active) (default: fast)
  --deep                    Also run the exhaustive BM25 pass and fuse it (slower)
  --single-resolution       One result per ranked unit; do not spend spare slots on finer regions of a prose document
  --document-resolution     Rank a prose document as one unit; do not rank its sections separately
  --max-context-bytes <n>   Output byte budget; 0 = unbounded (default: 24576)
  --reference-blocks all|container-map,signature-types,type-card
                            Turn reference blocks back on (off by default)
  --max-indexed-files <n>   Bound cold-search parsing to N files
  --index-all-files         Widen cold-search parsing to every file
  --cache-dir <path>        Override the committed-tree cache directory
  --no-cache                Disable the committed-tree cache

Examples:
  entire graph search --repo . --query "token refresh returns 401" --format text --top-k 8
  entire graph search --repo . --query "csv export ordering" --profile full

class Script:
    """Stands in for run_worker: answers each call with the next scripted output and records the calls."""

    def __init__(self, *outputs):

        self.calls.append(SimpleNamespace(goal=goal, type=output_type, **kwargs))
        output = self.outputs.pop(0) if self.outputs else None
        return output, {}

I built the opt-in coding workspace on isolated branch `codex/kernel-prototype` in commit `663df55`. The model selects a page or element, then runs JavaScript against a cleaned snapshot in a persistent, offline context of an existing browser.

On an invented 600-row page, the code cell and result used **381 characters** versus **13,001** returned by the existing `collect` tool. Those are payload sizes, not measured model tokens. Nineteen local tests pass. A runnable synthetic Qwen comparison is included, but I could not reach the local proxy from this agent’s environment, so end-to-end time, tokens, and quality remain unverified.

See the [prototype notes](/private/tmp/ehl-kernel-prototype/docs/code-kernel-prototype.md) and [Qwen benchmark](/private/tmp/ehl-kernel-prototype/dev/code_kernel_llm_bench.py).

# How a run works

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
logins.

## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox

RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.

1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
   provider takes your own key.
   Nothing done with these logins counts.
   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.

## Inside a run

1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
   returns:
   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
   provider's with your own key (below).
3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
     it again.
   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.

Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.

## LLM calls

Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.

The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:

```
$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
```

`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:

| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
| `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |

The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
(messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.

### Your key

Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
(OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.

With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
`OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
as `x-api-key`:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
```

A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:

```python
import os
from google import genai

client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],
    http_options={"base_url": os.environ["LLM_PROXY_URL"] + "/google"})
```

```javascript
import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai"

const client = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY,
  httpOptions: { baseUrl: process.env.LLM_PROXY_URL + "/google" } })
```

A request without a key of its own gets `401` "Add your <provider> API key to the request.", unless the
organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.

**Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
`$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
(prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
`x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
`401`.

A request body may be up to 32 MiB (`413` above that), enough for several full-screen screenshots and a long
context.

### How cost is measured

Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
A model too new for the platform's price list counts at the price OpenRouter lists for it, its long-context price
included. An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
`"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.

The models the platform hosts itself (`GET /v1/models/status` lists them with their prices) are free to use, never
charged; each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest.

### Team secrets

Team secrets are environment variables for your agent's run step in test runs and scored runs, such as
`OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:

```sh
curl -X PUT -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  --data '{"value": "sk-…"}' "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
curl -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets"   # names and dates only
curl -X DELETE -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
```

Values are encrypted, never shown again and redacted from run logs; saving a name again replaces its value.
Setup never receives them. Names are uppercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, and
cannot be platform variables (`CHALLENGE_*`, `*_BASE_URL`, `*_SERVER_URL`, `*_PROXY`, `LLM_PROXY_URL`,
`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `DISPLAY`, …). A team keeps at most 20; each value is 16 characters to 4 KB long.

## Scored run

Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run
ranks on the leaderboard. The final run at the end of the hackathon uses the same sandbox on a private dataset (see
[Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md#what-happens-next)). Runs are created from your uploaded package. The sandbox is
a Linux VM with a desktop at 1280×800, a **headful Chromium** already open with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on
`127.0.0.1:9222` (or up to four, see [Browsers](#browsers)) and these toolchains, ready for your user:

- **TypeScript and JavaScript:** Node 24 (runs `.ts` files directly), npm, pnpm and bun.
- **Python:** Python 3.12 and uv (`uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv run`); there is no system pip.
- **Rust:** stable Rust (1.99) with cargo. Fetch crates during setup; the run is offline except for the platform
  and the websites.
- gcc, make, git, curl and jq.

1. **Setup (not counted toward your time, up to 5 minutes):** your `setup` command runs with network access but without any credentials, e.g. to install dependencies.
2. **Model warm-up (not counted toward your time):** the models the platform hosts itself, when it offers any, scale
   to zero when nobody uses them, and waking one takes one to eight minutes. The platform wakes them as soon as your
   run leaves the queue and starts your run only once they're warm (at most 10 minutes after setup), so a cold start
   never counts toward your time. The run's log says when they're warm. While runs are active, the platform keeps
   them warm. `"models"` in `agent.json` lists the ones your agent system calls, by their `provider` id from
   `GET /v1/models/status` (the start page shows it too); the run waits for those alone, and `"models": []` starts it
   right after setup:

   ```json
   {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": []}
   ```

   Without it the run waits for every hosted model. Anything else, such as an unknown id, rejects the package with
   `Invalid agent.json: models: …` and the ids it takes. It decides only the wait: your run may call any hosted model
   whatever it lists, but one it didn't list may still be waking.

   **If a hosted model fails mid-run:** retry failed calls, as with any provider; a short outage is yours to ride out.
   If our models were down for most of the run (from the first failed call on, a 5xx from our model or a lost
   connection to it, at least 8 in 10 of the run's hosted-model calls failed, over at least half its time) and the run
   then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count toward ranking or
   any limit, and a scored run starts again once by itself. A
   run that answered keeps its result.
3. **Run (timed):** your `run` command starts with this environment. The clock starts here.

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `CHALLENGE_API_URL` | the API; read your task at `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` |
| `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` | the run token |
| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with this run's logins, as JSON: the same as `access` |
| `LLM_PROXY_URL` | `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` |
| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | for each model the platform hosts (`GET /v1/models/status`; the start page names them): its base URL through the proxy, under `$LLM_PROXY_URL/<provider>`, and the run token as its key |
| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
| `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |

| `MISTRAL_SERVER_URL`, `TOGETHER_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral`, `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
| your [team secrets](#team-secrets) | for example `OPENAI_API_KEY` with your own key |
| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222`, browser 1 |
| `CDP_URLS` | every browser's CDP URL in order, as a JSON array: `["http://127.0.0.1:9222"]` for one browser |
| `BROWSER_COUNT` | how many browsers the sandbox started: `1` unless `agent.json` asks for more |
| `DISPLAY` | `:1`, browser 1's screen; browser n is on `:n` |
| `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` (and lowercase) | `http://127.0.0.1:3128`, the only way out of the sandbox |
| `NO_PROXY` | `localhost,127.0.0.1` (CDP stays local) |

The platform sets no API key variables of its own, except the run-token placeholder for a provider the
organizers pay for (above). `setup` runs first, with network (install your dependencies there) but without the
run's variables or your team secrets, and nothing it starts survives into the run. The run itself reaches only our API and the challenge's websites,
through that proxy; Chromium is already configured to use it. A scored run of RFQ has 20 minutes; a run that
ends without an answer scores 0.

## Browsers

The sandbox starts one browser unless `agent.json` asks for more, up to four:

```json
{"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "browsers": 3}
```

`browsers` is a whole number from 1 to 4; anything else rejects the package with
`Invalid agent.json: browsers: must be a whole number from 1 to 4`. Browser n is its own headful Chromium with its
own profile, on display `:n` (1280×800) with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on port 9221 + n (9222 to 9225), behind
the same proxy as browser 1. All of them are ready before the clock starts. `CDP_URL` stays browser 1, `CDP_URLS` lists all of
them in order, and `BROWSER_COUNT` says how many there are. With three:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222` |
| `CDP_URLS` | `["http://127.0.0.1:9222","http://127.0.0.1:9223","http://127.0.0.1:9224"]` |
| `BROWSER_COUNT` | `3` |

**At most 4 browsers run at a time:** ask for up to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts
inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The scored sandbox enforces it:
any other browser the agent starts is stopped within seconds, and the run's logs say so with
`[platform] stopped a browser the agent started: at most 4 run at a time; use the browsers from CDP_URLS`. Every
browser then is one the platform can show and record: test runs show them side by side while they run, with a
recording of each afterwards.

On your own machine, developing with the scouting logins, `CDP_URLS` is not set and your agent starts its own
browsers.

Who has access to the coding tool? Like of the different agents / steps?

In the sandbox experiment, every browser worker created through `run_worker` has access: tender/specification navigation, ERP, mail search, and the form and signing workers. Brief and mail planners, standalone document readers, verification, and pricing calculations do not.

Each worker gets its own coding workspace, with state preserved across that worker’s code calls. It is closed when the worker finishes. Access is controlled by `AGENT_CODE_KERNEL=1`; the normal candidate has it off. This first experiment uses broad access so we can see where it helps, and the trace records which workers use it.

You are actually in a much better position than “not going well” sounds: **100/100 quality and currently 4th**. The gap is almost purely efficiency. Your present cost×time is roughly **21× the leader’s**, so this is now an architecture-optimization problem, not a reasoning problem. [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

The challenge rules give you a fairly large loophole—in the good sense: the **model has to choose what to investigate**, but once it has selected a page/result set/document, helpers may **extract it, paginate it, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms**. And you get **four browsers in parallel**. [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

### I would try this architecture

**1. Turn the agent into a tiny “control plane,” not the worker.**

Right now, if you're doing browser-agent loops like:

> screenshot → LLM → click → screenshot → LLM → click → ...

kill as much of that as possible.

Have the LLM make **one semantic decision** such as:

> “This is the latest applicable specification revision; extract its requirements.”

Then deterministic code takes over: DOM extraction, table pagination, ZIP/PDF parsing, etc. This is explicitly permitted after a model-selected target. [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

Think:

**LLM selects → code exhausts selected thing → LLM selects next semantic thing.**

Not:

**LLM drives every mouse movement.**

That could be the single biggest improvement.

---

### 2. Use all four browsers as a dependency DAG

You do **not** need to process the four sites sequentially; Atira explicitly says sites and positions can be investigated in parallel. [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

I would roughly do:

| Browser | Job |
|---|---|
| A | Tender + reference + positions + Q&A |
| B | Supplier portal + identify current spec + extract requirements |
| C | Mail: approvals / commercial records |
| D | ERP, immediately once Kataloggruppe + attributes arrive |

But don't make them four autonomous expensive agents.

Make them **four workers controlled by one central state object**.

As soon as Browser A finds the tender reference, emit it to C.  
As soon as B extracts requirement 10, emit it to D.  
As soon as A gets the final quantity for position 10, update pricing.  

You then overlap almost everything rather than waiting for “phase 1 complete.”

Your 7:33 is particularly suspicious here because the winner is doing the whole thing in **1:38**. They almost certainly aren't doing a long serial ReAct trajectory. [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

---

### 3. Do **zero LLM arithmetic**

This challenge is almost begging for a deterministic pricing engine.

Use `Decimal(..., ROUND_HALF_UP)` and encode all rules in code:

- quantity conversion
- price scales
- FX
- conditional discounts
- pooled stock
- carton rounding
- shared setup allocation
- marginal project bonus
- largest-remainder allocation
- metal-index date windows
- final unit price
- total

The LLM should merely produce facts such as:

```text
condition_group = KG2
discount_scope = base_and_surcharge
current_revision = REV_C
packaging_tariff = VP4
```

Your program calculates the answer.

The challenge specifically permits calculation helpers, and the numerical rules are completely specified. [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

This is also **more private-set robust** than letting Qwen repeatedly reason through pricing prose.

---

## The slightly more evil optimizations

### 4. Build a “semantic compiler”

Instead of asking an LLM to reason about all gathered evidence at the end, compile each selected document immediately into your own normalized IR:

```text
TenderState
  reference
  scenario_date
  positions[]

Position
  id
  qty
  kataloggruppe
  bore
  stroke
  pressure
  mounting
  certification
  condition_group
  packaging_key
  commitment_key
  ...
```

Mail becomes:

```text
AuthorityRecord {
   kind,
   tender_ref,
   effective_date,
   payload
}
```

ERP becomes:

```text
Material {
   id,
   attributes,
   stock,
   scale_prices,
   production_lead,
   ...
}
```

Once that IR exists, **there is no agent anymore**. The rest is a compiler.

I think this is a strong “elegant system” story too, which matters because private performance is followed by public performance and then **system elegance** in the final judging. [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

---

### 5. Ask models questions that can be answered in ~5 tokens

Qwen output costs considerably more than cached input: **$0.47/M output vs $0.016/M cached input**. [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

Don't ask:

> Analyze the page and explain which document is most likely...

Ask:

```text
Return one:
REV_A
REV_B
REV_C
```

Or use structured/tool responses:

```json
{"selected":2}
```

Likewise for navigation:

```json
{"action":"open","candidate":3}
```

No prose, no thoughts, no summaries.

You don't care whether Qwen can eloquently explain why `REV_C` is current.

---

### 6. Exploit prompt caching deliberately

Qwen cached input is almost **10× cheaper** than uncached input ($0.016/M vs $0.15/M). [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

Make the beginning of every Qwen request **byte-identical**:

```text
SYSTEM
challenge rules...
navigation policy...
schemas...
```

Then put the changing state at the very end.

Do **not** continually rewrite your giant system prompt/state summary.

Potentially:

```text
[STATIC 15k-token challenge/navigation prefix]
[DYNAMIC 500-token observation]
```

rather than repeatedly paying for a changing 15k context.

---

### 7. DOM-first, screenshot-last

Everything here is business software. Most of the information is text/tables/forms.

If your agent is feeding full 1280×800 screenshots into Qwen all the time, that's probably murder on both latency and cost.

Preferred hierarchy:

**DOM/accessibility text → selected element text → cropped screenshot → full screenshot**

Use vision only for genuinely awkward UI state: popup ambiguity, nested viewer controls, etc.

Clef is explicitly intended for cheap little decisions such as “which link?” / “is this the right document?” [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

---

### 8. Make Clef your reflex layer

Interesting possible hybrid:

**Clef = reflexes**  
**Qwen = semantics**

For example:

- “Which of these four buttons opens search?” → Clef
- “Is this page the current revision?” → Clef
- “Which one of these three mail results is about this tender?” → Clef

But:

- “Interpret this commercial clause.” → Qwen
- “Which technical amendment applies?” → Qwen

Clef output isn't priced, while Qwen output is. [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

I would benchmark it rather than blindly replacing everything, though—the input rate for Clef is actually higher than Qwen's.

---

## One especially promising idea: **LLM fan-out, not agent fan-out**

You have Qwen concurrency of **32 simultaneous calls**. [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

Suppose you have eight ERP candidates.

Don't do:

```text
agent considers candidate 1
agent considers candidate 2
...
```

Once the model has legitimately selected that ERP result set, your helper can extract it.

Then either **code compares exact structured attributes**—ideal—or fire tiny Qwen classification calls concurrently where interpretation remains necessary:

```text
candidate 1 match? Y/N
candidate 2 match? Y/N
...
```

Eight 300 ms-ish tasks in parallel rather than eight sequential reasoning turns.

Same for positions.

---

## And one thing I would *not* do

Don't overfit harder to the public websites to chase #1.

The private run changes:

- websites,
- software,
- layouts,
- navigation,
- site names,
- content,
- where information is split.

And **private-set performance matters most**. [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

So hardcoding selectors like “click the third sidebar item” might get you 50 seconds publicly and kill the actual competition.

The winning abstraction is likely:

> **generic model-guided semantic navigation + extremely aggressive deterministic execution once the model has chosen the target.**

That both obeys the rules and transfers.

### If I were error404.ai right now

I would spend the remaining optimization effort in this order:

1. **Move every calculation out of the LLM.**
2. **Run 4 browsers concurrently.**
3. **Replace per-click LLM loops with model-select → helper-extract.**
4. **Emit structured events immediately between browser workers.**
5. **Cut Qwen responses to tiny enums/JSON.**
6. **DOM/text instead of screenshots.**
7. **Parallelize per-position work.**
8. **Test Clef for trivial navigation decisions.**
9. **Optimize prompt caching.**
10. Only then experiment with smaller/fewer models.

Getting you from **7:33 → ~2:00–3:00** looks much more plausible than trying to squeeze your current sequential agent down incrementally. And because cost usually falls simultaneously when you remove agent turns, that attacks **both axes at once**—exactly what this leaderboard rewards. [Atira EHL Challenge](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq)

If your current implementation is roughly a browser-use/Playwright + Qwen loop, the **“semantic compiler” approach is probably the most interesting pivot I'd try tonight.**

# entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)

You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.

## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)

Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:

    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"

Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.

## Hard rules

1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.
2. READ focused source around the result. Widen the check when aliases, generated code, dynamic
   dispatch, or related implementations could matter.
3. Use graph follow-ups only when they answer a real question. For impact or callers, prefer:
       entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X
4. Make the smallest complete edit and check sibling sites or contracts when the task implies them.
5. VERIFY before stopping. Run the most focused relevant test, build, or reproduction available.
   If execution is unavailable, perform a bounded source-level verification and state the limit.
6. Prefer precise queries and line ranges, but never trade resolution for fewer turns.
7. Feature-detect before relying on semantic relations:
       entire graph capabilities --json

## When NOT to use the graph

If the task already names the exact file and it is small, just read it — the graph saves tokens
by eliminating exploration; when there is nothing to explore, skip it.

## Reference

    locate  ->  entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "..."
    impact  ->  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X   (one shot: callers, callees, type consumers, data flow, co-change, siblings)
    callers ->  entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in
    change  ->  entire graph diff --base A --head B --json
    detect  ->  entire graph capabilities --json   (inventory-only languages have no relations)
    stats   ->  entire graph stats --repo .        (human-facing token-savings report; not part of your workflow — do not run it unless asked)

Currently, **every browser worker gets coding access when `AGENT_CODE_KERNEL=1`**:

| Agent / step | Coding access |
|---|---|
| Tender navigation and positions | Yes |
| Specification navigation | Yes |
| ERP search and detail navigation | Yes |
| Mail search and navigation | Yes |
| Form filling and signing/TAN | Yes |
| Planning agents | No |
| Standalone document and record readers | No |
| Verification agents | No |
| Pricing engine | Already deterministic Python |

Each worker has **its own persistent workspace**, closed when that worker finishes. It executes JavaScript against a cleaned snapshot of the selected page; it cannot directly manipulate the live page or access the network.

The latest prototype provides `analyze_selected` and `finish_from_code`, which can return a validated final result directly. Coding remains opt-in; the main implementation is unchanged.

**The sandbox run actually used it:** two calls during mail research and four during signing, finishing with **100/100 quality**. However, overall calls and input tokens increased. I’d next restrict access to dense extraction tasks—tables and documents—where it has a clearer chance of saving work.

# Model-directed code workspace prototype

Set `AGENT_CODE_KERNEL=1` to give each browser worker an optional `analyze_selected(ref, code)` tool. The model still chooses the page, record, search and element. The tool copies that one selected visible DOM subtree into an inert document and runs its JavaScript against it. `state` persists across cells in the worker, so the model can keep a compact derived table and query it again without sending the full page through its prompt. Every worker gets its own context; it closes when the worker ends. Default is off.

The same option also offers `finish_from_code(ref, code)` as a PydanticAI output function. Code must **return** a JSON object matching the worker's typed result; the function validates it, checks grounding against the selected page, and ends that worker. The ordinary `final_result` output remains available. This aims to remove the extra model turn that copies a code result into a typed answer, and may discourage repeated checks. It does not replace navigation, form filling, signing or the existing standalone record/document readers: only `run_worker` gets this output function so far.

Example on an invented register (the model supplies this code):

```javascript
state.rows = [...doc.querySelectorAll('tr')].map(row =>
  [...row.cells].map(cell => cell.textContent.trim()));
return state.rows.filter(row => row[1] === '40 mm').map(row => row[0]);
```

This uses an extra context of an **existing provided browser**, never a new browser process. The context is offline, blocks HTTP requests and WebSockets, and has no site cookies or opener. It receives inert HTML with scripts, handlers, external resources, password inputs and hidden elements removed. Attributes are limited to visible or structural semantics such as labels, titles, dates, table spans, values of visible inputs and our generated element refs; hidden `data-*`, URLs and form metadata are omitted. It cannot act on the live site through the tool. Snapshot reads, cell time, code length, output length and number of cells are bounded. A selected snapshot's visible text is added to the worker's grounding record.

This is a scoped browser JavaScript workspace, not an OS security boundary. Hancas's Python `KernelExecutor` relies on Apptainer and bubblewrap isolation; copying its bare Python fallback into this challenge package would let model-authored code read process secrets and files. A Python kernel is possible only with a verified sandbox substrate in the challenge environment. The current prototype also does not inspect cross-origin frames through a parent page snapshot; choose a ref in the frame, which `locate` can resolve.

## Synthetic microbenchmark

Run `cd agent && uv run --no-sync python ../dev/code_kernel_bench.py`. The fixture is an invented 600-row register. On one local run:

| Method | Model-visible characters | `chars / 4` token proxy | Local browser time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Existing `observe` + `read_more` | 37,219 in 3 chunks | 9,305 | 10.3 ms to observe |
| Existing `collect` | 13,001; first 200 rows | 3,251 | 28.1 ms |
| One code cell + result | 381 | 96 | 21.6 ms snapshot + 36.0 ms cold / 2.5 ms warm cell |

The token proxy is **not measured model tokens**. The code cell has to be written by the model and the current worker already has an initial page view, so these figures do not imply a 97% run-level saving. They show the opportunity when a model needs a narrow answer from a dense selected page. One Qwen A/B is reported below. No public challenge run has tested quality, actual tokens or end-to-end time. Before enabling by default, run further synthetic comparisons and a public test run, then compare quality and whole-run token/call/time records.

The main risk is extra model effort: writing code can cost more turns than `collect` on short lists, and arbitrary code can return a plausible but wrong filter. Keep it optional for dense pages and verify decisive facts against the selected evidence.

For an actual model comparison with a local Atira proxy, set `QWEN_BASE_URL` and `QWEN_API_KEY` from the proxy and run `cd agent && uv run --no-sync python ../dev/code_kernel_llm_bench.py --out /private/tmp/kernel-llm-bench`. It asks Qwen for a complete filter of an invented 350-row register once with the existing tools and once with the code tool; each result reports correctness, requests, input/output tokens and wall time. `--mode kernel` repeats only that path. `--out` keeps the traces in separate `baseline/` and `kernel/` directories. The synthetic script enables detailed code-cell tracing; normal runs do not record code and returned text.

The first local Qwen comparison on the original prompt used 12 calls on each path: the existing tools failed the 12-call cap (18.5 s, 44,166 input and 356 output tokens), while the code path found all 19 matches (23.6 s, 46,165 input and 1,423 output tokens). The code model tried nine cells, including one after its eight-cell allowance. This establishes a quality gain on that fixture but no time or token gain. The prompt and trace-preservation changes after that run need a new comparison before interpreting their effect.

A preserved trace from a later run showed the code path had the complete correct result by its second cell, then spent six more cells rechecking the same snapshot. The worker now has a generic stopping rule: return the typed answer once a selected snapshot yields all requested facts; repeat only after an error, an unresolved requirement or contradictory new evidence. Code results also survive later page views in worker history. Those changes still need a measured model rerun.

The tool copies that one selected visible DOM subtree into an inert document and runs its JavaScript against it. `state` persists across cells in the worker, so the model can keep a compact derived table and query it again without sending the full page through its prompt. Every worker gets its own context; it closes when the worker ends. Default is off.

The same option also offers `finish_from_code(ref, code)` as a PydanticAI output function. Code must **return** a JSON object matching the worker's typed result; the function validates it, checks grounding against the selected page, and ends that worker. The ordinary `final_result` output remains available. This aims to remove the extra model turn that copies a code result into a typed answer, and may discourage repeated checks. It does not replace navigation, form filling, signing or the existing standalone record/document readers: only `run_worker` gets this output function so far.

Example on an invented register (the model supplies this code):

```javascript
state.rows = [...doc.querySelectorAll('tr')].map(row =>
  [...row.cells].map(cell => cell.textContent.trim()));
return state.rows.filter(row => row[1] === '40 mm').map(row => row[0]);
```

This uses an extra context of an **existing provided browser**, never a new browser process. The context is offline, blocks HTTP requests and WebSockets, and has no site cookies or opener. It receives inert HTML with scripts, handlers, external resources, password inputs and hidden elements removed. Attributes are limited to visible or structural semantics such as labels, titles, dates, table spans, values of visible inputs and our generated element refs; hidden `data-*`, URLs and form metadata are omitted. It cannot act on the live site through the tool. Snapshot reads, cell time, code length, output length and number of cells are bounded. A selected snapshot's visible text is added to the worker's grounding record.

This is a scoped browser JavaScript workspace, not an OS security boundary. Hancas's Python `KernelExecutor` relies on Apptainer and bubblewrap isolation; copying its bare Python fallback into this challenge package would let model-authored code read process secrets and files. A Python kernel is possible only with a verified sandbox substrate in the challenge environment. The current prototype also does not inspect cross-origin frames through a parent page snapshot; choose a ref in the frame, which `locate` can resolve.

| Existing `observe` + `read_more` | 37,219 in 3 chunks | 9,305 | 10.3 ms to observe |
| Existing `collect` | 13,001; first 200 rows | 3,251 | 28.1 ms |
| One code cell + result | 381 | 96 | 21.6 ms snapshot + 36.0 ms cold / 2.5 ms warm cell |

Team error404.ai at the Atira EHL Challenge ("From RFQ to bid", challenge id `rfq`, event 10 Oct 2026, up to 5 people
per team). The agent lives in `agent/` and is built on the Atira starter kit. Keep the GitHub repo private.

## Status and layout

- `docs/plan.md`: framework decision (pydantic-ai on Qwen, no LangGraph, no browser-agent framework), module layout,
  site scouting notes and the roadmap v0 to v5. Read it first. Its scouting notes describe public-1 only: they inform
  generic helpers, they must never become hardcoded paths, labels, values or prompt text (the private final run uses
  other software, layouts and data).
- `agent/` (v2, reaches quality 100 in the sandbox): `agent.py` `solve()` warms all site sessions in the background,
  reads the brief (`briefing.py`), runs research (`orchestrator.py` with `board.py`, `verify.py`; workers in
  `research.py` spec + ERP, `research_tender.py`, `research_mail.py`; tools in `site_tools.py`), computes the answer
  with `calc.py`, and enters/signs it via `submit.py` + `configurator.py` (positions without a complete answer are
  omitted; the bid is always signed). Harness: `llm.py` (per-mode deadlines; opt-in `LLM_STREAM_WATCHDOG`),
  `extract.py`, `browser_tools.py` (`SiteSession`: resilient starts, `revive()`), `worker.py`, `tracing.py` (run
  summary printed at the end, since the platform keeps only the last ~260 output lines), `loopwatch.py`, `clef.py`
  (off unless `AGENT_CLEF=1`). `agent.json` asks for 4 browsers.
- `dev/`: `smoke.py` (v0 check), `run-local.sh`, `test-run.sh`, `track.py` (run log), `soak.py` (keeps N sandbox test
  runs of HEAD going: `python3 dev/soak.py --slots 2`), `local-soak.sh` (local runs up to signing, scored by
  `checks/score.py`), `robustness.py` (renamed sites, reworded brief), `research_check*.py`, `configurator_check.py`.
- `checks/` (gitignored): hand-derived public-1 answer and `python3 checks/score.py <answer.json>`; never copy its
  values into `agent/`.
- Submitting: export committed code with `git archive HEAD agent` into a temp dir and submit/test from there, so
  untracked work in progress never reaches the package reviewer. Test runs under 20 min can be promoted to a
  submission (run page button or `POST /v1/runs/<run_id>/promotion`); the promoted run becomes the latest submission.
- Branches `submitted/<sub id>` mark the exact code of each submission. Use `git status` and `atira status` for the
  current state; do not trust dated numbers in this file.
- The scouting logins are shared by all teams: the bid wizard is per browser session (safe), but webmail TANs and ERP
  sessions collide, so local runs stop before the TAN (`AGENT_STOP_BEFORE_SIGN=1`) and run one at a time.

## Tracking runs

Record every test run and submission; they go to `experiments/runs.jsonl` (append-only, `merge=union`, committed with
the change it measured). Local runs go to `experiments/local-runs.jsonl` (gitignored). `python3 dev/track.py report`
renders both to `docs/experiments.md` (gitignored). From the repo root:

```sh
dev/test-run.sh v1 "what changed" [experiment]    # sandbox test run, followed to the end, score recorded
dev/run-local.sh v1 "what changed" [experiment]   # local, headless; needs `atira models proxy`
python3 dev/track.py platform <sub_id> --version v1 --experiment NAME --note "..."   # after `atira submit`
```

`version` is the base being measured (v1, v2, ...); `experiment` names what a run varies on top of it (e.g.
`thinking-off-forms`, `model-<name>`, `4-browsers`), so variants of one version compare side by side. Environment
overrides (`AGENT_*`, `LLM_*`, `THINKING*`, `MAX_STEPS*`) are recorded, with secrets redacted. `atira test-run`
uploads untracked files too, so the recorded commit is a pointer; `atira package <id>` shows the exact upload.
When a run taught something (a failure mode, a speed-up, a score change), add a bullet to `docs/learned.md`. Notes
never contain credentials or values copied from the sites.

## Platform docs (source of truth; re-read, they change)

Base `https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai`. Public pages (home, start, challenge, leaderboard, team profiles) are also
Markdown via `.md`; docs are `/docs/<name>.md`.

- `/start.md`, `/challenges/rfq.md` (29 bid rules, answer schema), `/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md`
- `/docs/fair-play.md`, `scoring.md`, `submitting.md`, `run-contract.md`, `building-an-agent.md`, `cli.md`, `api.md`,
  `mcp.md`, `faq.md`, `demo-day.md`; `/openapi.json`, `/llms.txt`, `/llms-full.txt` (all docs in one file)
- Announcements need a token: `curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)" https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/v1/announcements`
- Submission deadline and prizes are not in the docs: ask the organizers. Demo day: best teams run live on stage, so
  keep a one-line start command (`atira test-run ./agent`) and a fallback recording.

The scouting logins are deliberately NOT stored here: run `atira scout`. Never write them, or anything copied from
the sites, into code, prompts, fixtures, notes or fallbacks.

## Fair play (an AI reviewer rejects or flags these)

- No hardcoded scenario values (tender refs, material numbers, prices, discounts, logins, TANs), not even as defaults,
  fallbacks or in prompts. Facts the brief states for every scenario (e.g. the sales director's mailbox) are fine.
- No pre-solving, by you or an AI assistant, put into the package. Hand-derived expectations stay outside `agent/`.
- Must be agentic: a model chooses where to go, what to search and what matters. Rejected: a fixed click path (model
  unused or only a fallback), or a crawler/helper that gathers all evidence before model-directed investigation.
  Allowed helpers: parse a page or document the model chose, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate,
  validate, retry, fill forms. Several agents and parallel browsers are fine.
- Only the platform API, the four sites and the model proxy; no local models; no own browsers in the sandbox (use the
  provided 1 to 4, tabs and contexts are free).
- Do not write notes meant to steer the reviewer. Outcomes: passed; flagged (runs, but hidden from the leaderboard
  until an organizer passes it); rejected (no runs).

## The task and its traps

One signed bid, entered in the tender portal's configurator and signed with a TAN from the webmail. Site ids are
public-1 names; the private set renames and re-splits sites, so never branch code on siteId, URL or layout.

| Site | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| Tender portal | Tender, bill of quantities, bidder Q&A (the hub: quantity changes, withdrawals, scoped spec amendments, Konditionsgruppe, packaging, commitment and setup-pool keys), configurator |
| Supplier portal | Buyer's spec and revisions (oldest shown first; use the one marked current) |
| ERP | Materials and status, stock, lead times, price conditions with validity and scales, pieces per carton, allocation mass |
| Webmail | Director's discount approval, TAN, authority mails (look-alikes, superseded, archive) |

Read all 29 rules in `challenges/rfq.md` before writing prompts or tools. Highest-impact traps:

- **Authority and time (21):** per key, the latest record dated no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender
  reference, from the right sender (technik, logistik, finanzen, kalkulation + bidder mailbox domain). Future-dated and
  unrelated records never apply; a failed condition does not revive an older record.
- **no_bid (3, 8, 16):** if any position has no exactly matching active material (after amendments and the "nutzbarer
  Weg" derivation, rule 20), send `no_bid`, no positions, `total_net` 0 (schema still requires `discount_percent`; a
  conditional approval means 0 %). Omitting positions is not a substitute (rule 9).
- **Sign and submit:** saving alone scores nothing. Partial bids use "Position auslassen" and are still signed.
- **Per position vs per material:** price scales per position; stock pooled per material (15); delivery commitments
  per position, only if the material matches and pooled demand is within the inclusive ceiling (24).
- **Rounding:** HALF_UP, at the steps the rules name: FX-converted base price to cents (22), discount threshold and
  bonus aggregate to cents (16, 26), then the final unit price once from unrounded per-piece components (27).
  Breakdown fields are reports, not inputs. Bonus split: largest remainders (26); setup pool: the cent-allocation rule
  stated in the Ruestpools mail (25).
- **Reporting:** `surcharge_per_unit` is before discount and covers mass surcharge plus ordinary and allocated setup;
  setup and packaging are never discounted; blank = unanswered, `0.00` = known zero; `rebate_total` is per position.
- **Conditional discount (16):** threshold uses undiscounted scale prices, no surcharge or setup, inclusive; on failure
  0 %, never an older approval. Metal index: the rate whose window contains the scenario date (28).
- Positions are matched by number; extras or duplicates cost one position's share; money is compared to the cent.

## Runs, ranking, winning

Details live in `submitting.md`, `run-contract.md`, `scoring.md`, `faq.md`. What bites:

- Test run (`atira test-run ./agent --follow`): 2 h, public data, shows per-part points, never on the leaderboard.
  Scored (`atira submit ./agent`): AI review, then one 20-minute run, one submission in flight per team (else 429).
- Time runs from the start of the run command to the accepted answer. 202 is final (even if wrong); 400 lists issues
  and the clock keeps running; validate against `answer_schema` first. Submit about 90 s before `expires_at` (the kit's
  `run.seconds_left` helps); platform docs only say "about a minute". A run without an answer scores 0.
- Setup has network and 5 min (untimed), but no run variables or secrets, and nothing it starts survives. The timed run
  reaches only the platform, sites and model proxy (`HTTP(S)_PROXY`, honour it in custom clients). Send your own
  User-Agent (default Python agents get 403 "Error 1010").
- `agent.json`: `setup`, `run`, `models` (list every hosted model used, e.g. `["qwen","clef"]`), `browsers` 1 to 4.
  Package: 20 MB compressed and uncompressed, 2,000 files, 5 MB per file, `.gitignore` honoured, no secrets inside.
  Own model keys are team secrets (names: capitals, digits, underscore, letter first, max 20, no platform names).
- Order: eligible (right tender reference), then quality 0 to 100, then lower cost x time (floors $0.01, 1 s). A wrong
  bid/no_bid decision costs quality, not eligibility (75 of 100 in a no_bid case). Weights: rule 29.
- Winners: private-dataset final run of our LATEST submission that PASSED review (not the best), then public
  leaderboard, then elegance. So: never tune to public-1; every passing `atira submit` replaces the final candidate,
  even a worse one, so confirm with the team first. `atira final --best-of 3` (before the final starts) allows three
  attempts (own-key cost up to 3x); private runs show no score breakdown.
- Models: hosted Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (`QWEN_BASE_URL/KEY`, 32 concurrent) and Clef (`CLEF_*`, 16 concurrent) are free
  but add a SIMULATED price to run cost; own-key calls are metered at provider prices through the proxy. Measured
  Qwen behaviour (thinking flag, schema cold start, caching) is in `docs/plan.md`.

## Dev loop

```sh
curl -fsSL https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.sh | sh    # CLI; the installer provides Node 24 if missing
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" && atira login           # `atira upgrade` if a command is unknown
(cd agent && uv sync && uv run playwright install chromium)
atira models proxy                       # terminal 1 (port 8765)
eval "$(atira scout --env)"              # terminal 2: scouting logins + model vars
(cd agent && uv run --no-sync python agent.py)   # local run, nothing submitted
(cd agent && uv run python -m unittest discover -s tests)
atira test-run ./agent --dry-run         # what would upload
atira test-run ./agent --follow          # sandbox run with score breakdown
```

Debugging: `atira logs <run> --follow`, `atira status [id]`, `atira package <id> --out dir`, `atira cancel <run>`; every
command takes `--json`. `claude mcp add atira -- atira mcp` gives `diagnose_run`, `run_logs`, `run_llm_calls`,
`run_screenshot`, `compare_runs` and more (`mcp.md`). Use the score breakdown to localise errors (zero surcharge
points can come from mass surcharge, setup or metal index inputs). A cancelled scored run ends its submission (ignored
by the leaderboard), so you may resubmit. Missing "OpenAI key" 401s mean no provider key arrived (team secret).
On macOS, python.org Python needs `Install Certificates.command` or `SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/cert.pem`.

## Team conventions

- Git: commit author `josteng <jonas@stenglein.dev>`; imperative subject of at most 50 characters, body as short `-`
  bullets; no attribution trailers (no Co-Authored-By, no session links); never stage anything under `.claude/`;
  never push or open a PR without asking first.
- Never put real credentials, personal data or site values in tests, fixtures, docs or comments; invent placeholders.

def _common_edges(texts: list[str]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Lines shared at the start and at the end of every text (site chrome), to show them only once."""
    lines = [t.splitlines() for t in texts]
    if len(lines) < 2:
        return 0, 0
    head = 0
    while all(len(x) > head for x in lines) and len({x[head] for x in lines}) == 1:
        head += 1
    tail = 0
    while all(len(x) > head + tail for x in lines) and len({x[-1 - tail] for x in lines}) == 1:
        tail += 1
    return head, tail

# How a run works

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
logins.

## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox

RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.

1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
   provider takes your own key.
   Nothing done with these logins counts.
   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.

## Inside a run

1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
   returns:
   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
   provider's with your own key (below).
3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
     it again.
   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.

Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.

## LLM calls

Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.

The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:

```
$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
```

`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:

| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
| `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |

The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
(messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.

### Your key

Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
(OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.

With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
`OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
as `x-api-key`:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
```

A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:

```python
import os
from google import genai

client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],
    http_options={"base_url": os.environ["LLM_PROXY_URL"] + "/google"})
```

```javascript

const client = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY,
  httpOptions: { baseUrl: process.env.LLM_PROXY_URL + "/google" } })
```

organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.

**Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
`$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
(prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
`x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
`401`.

A request body may be up to 32 MiB (`413` above that), enough for several full-screen screenshots and a long
context.

### How cost is measured

Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
A model too new for the platform's price list counts at the price OpenRouter lists for it, its long-context price
included. An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
`"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.

The models the platform hosts itself (`GET /v1/models/status` lists them with their prices) are free to use, never
charged; each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest.

`OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:

```sh

curl -X DELETE -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
```

Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run

    """Open each chosen URL in a temporary tab of the session's browser context, side by side, and keep its text."""

    async def one(url: str) -> str:
        tab = SiteSession(session.site, session.context, session.trace)
        page = await session.context.new_page()
        tab._watch(page)

            await tab._goto(url)
            await expand_collapsed(page)

            # An embedded document that did not render in place (e.g. a lazy reading pane) is part of the chosen
            # page: open it on its own and add its text.
            for src in EMPTY_FRAME.findall(view)[:3]:

                view += f"\n[frame {src} opened]\n" + await tab.look()

"""Reader integration on invented selected evidence and real child processes."""
import sys
import unittest
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))

from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic_ai import ModelRetry
from pydantic_ai.messages import ModelResponse, ToolCallPart
from pydantic_ai.models.function import FunctionModel

from reader_kernel import read_with_code


class Answer(BaseModel):
    ids: list[str]


class ReaderKernelTest(unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase):
    async def test_source_stays_out_of_prompt_and_state_reaches_typed_finish(self):
        source = 'invented heading\n' + ('ordinary row\n' * 150) + 'MATCH-Z7\n'
        calls = 0

        def respond(messages, info):
            nonlocal calls
            calls += 1
            if calls == 1:
                self.assertNotIn('MATCH-Z7', str(messages))
                return ModelResponse(parts=[ToolCallPart('analyze_python',
                    {'code': "import re\nstate['ids'] = re.findall(r'MATCH-\\w+', text)\nlen(state['ids'])"},
                    tool_call_id='1')])
            return ModelResponse(parts=[ToolCallPart('finish_from_python',
                {'code': "{'ids': state['ids']}"}, tool_call_id='2')])

        def validate(answer):
            if any(value not in source for value in answer.ids):
                raise ModelRetry('Ungrounded identifier')
            return answer

        result = await read_with_code(Answer, 'Copy matching identifiers.',
                                     'Find identifiers.\n' + source, source,
                                     model=FunctionModel(respond), settings={}, validate=validate)
        self.assertEqual(result.ids, ['MATCH-Z7'])
        self.assertEqual(calls, 2)

    async def test_ungrounded_code_answer_retries(self):
        calls = 0

        def respond(messages, info):
            nonlocal calls
            calls += 1
            value = 'Invented-Wrong9' if calls == 1 else 'Selected-A1'
            return ModelResponse(parts=[ToolCallPart('finish_from_python',
                {'code': repr({'ids': [value]})}, tool_call_id=str(calls))])

        def validate(answer):
            if answer.ids != ['Selected-A1']:
                raise ModelRetry('Value is absent from selected evidence')
            return answer

        result = await read_with_code(Answer, 'Copy identifiers.', 'Selected-A1', 'Selected-A1',
                                     model=FunctionModel(respond), settings={}, validate=validate)
        self.assertEqual(result.ids, ['Selected-A1'])
        self.assertEqual(calls, 2)

# Persistent Python reader prototype The [run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md) says the timed VM has Python 3.12 and `uv`; its setup step can install Python packages. The [fair-play rules](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md) allow code helpers to parse a document or page that the model chose. They do not specify Apptainer, bubblewrap or another nested OS sandbox. Thus **Python execution is available**, while nested isolation for model-authored Python is **unverified**. A public sandbox test of the child protocol and actual package review would still be needed before deployment. `agent/python_kernel.py` implements a small persistent child process in the same VM. A reader creates `PythonKernel()`, then calls `await kernel.execute(html=selected_html, text=selected_text, code=model_code)` or `await kernel.execute_json(...)` for a typed result, and calls `await kernel.close()` in `finally`. `html` and `text` cross a local JSONL pipe, never the model prompt or model-authored code string. Globals, imports and `state` persist across cells for that reader. The child uses the agent's Python interpreter, so standard-library imports and packages installed during setup are available. It starts no browser and uses no network endpoint. The child receives a minimal environment without run tokens, site credentials or model keys. It runs with Python `-I`, a private working directory, a three-second cell timeout and a process-group kill on timeout. Input, output and cell count are capped. This limits accidental exposure and runaway work; **it is not an OS security boundary**. Python code in the same VM can still attempt to read files or access network endpoints allowed by the challenge sandbox. The platform's own VM/network isolation, fair-play rules and the model's selected-source provenance remain relevant. Five invented-fixture tests cover persistent state/imports, JSON output, noninheritance of a synthetic run token, timeout cleanup and the eight-cell cap. The original grounding validators remain in place for both Python-produced and direct typed answers. Full source text reaches the child process, so a missing HTML snapshot does not itself discard facts.

The main integration gap is snapshot matching: specification pages are stored under stripped text but read under unstripped text. ERP and tender-position readers use combined text, so they also receive a text wrapper instead of selected HTML. Even when HTML matches, the snapshot omits rendered iframe contents that the reader text may contain. Readers should treat `text` as the complete evidence.

One quality risk merits a fallback before wider use: sources above the child’s 250,000-character limit cannot be analyzed, while the model sees only a 1,200-character preview. Route those reads through the existing reader.

# What we tried and learned

One bullet per experiment or failure: what changed, what happened, what we keep. Written by hand; run data is in
`experiments/runs.jsonl` (render it with `python3 dev/track.py report`).

- v0-starter test run: the starter kit's `solve()` stub exits without an answer; the sandbox scores that 0 and
  ineligible after 4 s.
- v1 local (first signed bid): the configurator worker needed 36 requests and 433 s for a bid with every position
  omitted; about 230 s of that went to the TAN round trips (153 s to 385 s).
- TAN loop: each TAN request invalidates the previous TAN, and the mail worker was started 6 times (2 hit the 8-request
  limit) before a fresh TAN reached the signing step in time. Fetch the TAN right after requesting it, in one sequence.
- Tokens: 247k input for a bid without positions, nearly all in the configurator worker; trim page views before v2.
- TAN lookup fixes: never put wall-clock time in a goal (the sites run on the scenario clock, so a TAN "requested at
  <today>" never shows up); "newest" is the highest request number. Short lookups run without note(), so the model
  returns its result instead of noting it and searching on.
- v1 first test run crashed at import: `llm.py` imported `httpx`, but openai 3.x depends on `httpx2`; the local venv
  still had a stale `httpx` from openai 2.x. Run `uv sync` after dependency changes so local matches the sandbox.
- v1 first scored test run: quality 10 (decision 5 + reference 5), eligible, 3.4 min, $0.022. Discount, total and

- TAN loop: each TAN request invalidates the previous TAN, and the mail worker was started 6 times (2 hit the 8-request
  limit) before a fresh TAN reached the signing step in time. Fetch the TAN right after requesting it, in one sequence.
- Tokens: 247k input for a bid without positions, nearly all in the configurator worker; trim page views before v2.
- TAN lookup fixes: never put wall-clock time in a goal (the sites run on the scenario clock, so a TAN "requested at

  returns its result instead of noting it and searching on.
